query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partially replacing Hf with additional Zr in the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy will lower its overall density without sacrificing its room‐temperature and high‐temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of about 10.21 g/cm³, exhibiting ~1600 MPa yield strength at room temperature and ~855 MPa at elevated temperature.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by partially substituting Hf with Zr (e.g., form a modified alloy Hf1-xZrxMoTaTiZr with an optimized value of x) to reduce the heavy-element content.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests conducted at room temperature (for tensile/ductility performance) and at 1000 °C (for high-temperature yield strength verification) under loading conditions comparable to previous RHEA experiments.
generation.structural_mediator: The single-phase body-centered cubic solid solution is maintained with similar lattice distortion and grain structure.
generation.mechanism: Zr has a lower atomic mass than Hf, so its increased fraction decreases the overall density while preserving the solid solution strengthening. This maintains dislocation-mediated deformation mechanisms (e.g., edge and screw dislocations) that are responsible for high yield strengths at both room and elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy’s density is expected to drop significantly (targeting a reduction of roughly 10–15%), while the room-temperature and high-temperature yield strengths remain comparable to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr (i.e., within 10% of 1600 MPa at RT and 855 MPa at 1000 °C) and ductility is preserved.
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with density ≈10.21 g/cm³, ~1600 MPa yield strength at room temperature, and ~855 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C.
generation.boundary: Tests are confined to room temperature loading and tensile testing at 1000 °C; the BCC phase should be maintained without formation of deleterious secondary phases under these thermal and mechanical conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum replacement fraction of Hf with Zr is not fully established; there is potential uncertainty that excessive substitution may weaken high-temperature performance or alter deformation mechanisms.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two alloy batches: the baseline as-cast HfMoTaTiZr and a modified alloy with a predetermined partial substitution of Hf by Zr (e.g., Hf0.5Zr0.5MoTaTiZr). Subject both alloys to identical casting and homogenization treatments. Conduct density measurements, room-temperature tensile tests, and high-temperature tensile tests at 1000 °C.
measurements: Room-temperature yield strength (MPa) and ductility (% elongation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy exhibits less than a 10% reduction in density relative to the baseline or if any of the key mechanical properties (yield strength at RT and 1000 °C) deviate by more than 10% from those of the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, then the hypothesis that the substitution can reduce density without sacrificing performance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Conclusions: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen
